Purpose

The purpose of this assessment probe is to elicit students’ ideas about complete circuits                                                                                                                                                         Energy
involving light bulbs. The probe reveals whether students recognize the pathway of
                                                   An
electricity in a complete circuit, including its path through a light bulb, to light a bulb using
only one strip of wire and a battery.

Explanation                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  Electricity:
The best answer is A­—one strip of wire.
                                                   C:
If you closely examine a flashlight bulb, you will see two small wires sticking up in the bulb
that are connected by a very fine wire called a filament. The two wires on either side of the                                                                                                                                                         Lessonfilament extend downward into the base of the bulb, where you cannot see them through
the metal casing surrounding the base of the bulb. One of these wires goes down to the very
bottom of the base (the pointed end). The other wire is connected to the side of the metal
base (sometimes the side is ridged so that it can screw into a socket). Knowing where these
wires end up on the base of the bulb (the tip and the side) is necessary in order to use one
wire to make a circuit that lights a bulb. The battery, wire, and bulb need to be connected
in such a way as to form a complete circuit. To do this, hold the end of the wire against the
negative terminal (the bottom of the battery or smooth end). The other end of the wire
should touch or wrap around the side of the metal casing that forms the base of the light
bulb. With the wire wrapped around the metal side of the bulb and the other end touching
the bottom of the battery, touch the tip of the base of the light bulb to the positive terminal
(bumpy end), and the bulb will light. The light bulb lights with just one wire because the
electricity flows out of the negative terminal (bottom of the battery), through the wire, into
the wire that is attached to the side of the metal casing on the base of the bulb, up through
that wire inside the bulb, across the filament, and down the other wire inside the bulb,
where it is attached to the point on the base of the bulb that touches the positive terminal
(the bump) of the battery, completing a full circuit.

Be aware, however, that students can choose the best answer, “one wire,” and still have
an incorrect configuration of a circuit. For example, some students may touch one end
of the wire to the battery and the other to the bulb, thinking the energy from the battery   1
will flow through the wire to the bulb. Students who choose two wires as their answer           Set
may understand that a complete circuit is needed, but may not understand the internal
architecture of a light bulb.                                                                                                                                                                                                            Activity

Greenhouse Gases

Carbon dioxide (CO2) is one of the greenhouse gases. It consists of one carbon atom with                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               Greenhouse
an oxygen atom bonded to each side. When its atoms are bonded tightly together, the
carbon dioxide molecule can absorb infrared radiation and the molecule starts to vibrate.        The
Eventually, the vibrating molecule will emit the radiation again, and it will likely be        I:
absorbed by yet another greenhouse gas molecule. This absorption-emission-absorption
cycle serves to keep the heat near the surface, effectively insulating the surface from the cold                                                                                                                                                         Lesson
of space.

Carbon dioxide, water vapor (H2O), methane (CH4), nitrous oxide (N20) and a few other
gases are greenhouse gases. They all are molecules composed of more than two component
atoms, bound loosely enough together to be able to vibrate with the absorption of heat. The
major components of the atmosphere (N2 and O2) are two-atom molecules too tightly bound
together to vibrate and thus they do not absorb heat and contribute to the greenhouse effect.

Greenhouse Effect
Atmospheric scientists first used the term ‘greenhouse effect’ in the early 1800s. At
that time, it was used to describe the naturally occurring functions of trace gases in the
atmosphere and did not have any negative connotations. It was not until the mid-1950s
that the term greenhouse effect was coupled with concern over climate change. In recent
decades, we often hear the term greenhouse effect used in somewhat negative ways. The
negative concerns are related to the possible impacts of an enhanced greenhouse effect. It
is important to remember that without the greenhouse effect, life on earth as we know it
would not be possible.

While the Earth’s temperature is dependent upon the greenhouse-like action of the
atmosphere, the amount of heating and cooling are strongly influenced by several factors
just as greenhouses are affected by various factors.

In the atmospheric greenhouse effect, the type of surface that sunlight first encounters is the
most important factor. Forests, grasslands, ocean surfaces, ice caps, deserts, and cities all
absorb, reflect, and radiate radiation differently. Sunlight falling on a white glacier surface   2
strongly reflects back into space, resulting in minimal heating of the surface and lower          Set
atmosphere. Sunlight falling on a dark desert soil is strongly absorbed, on the other hand,                    Activity

What is the difference between energy efficiency and energy conservation? Energy
efficiency and energy conservation are two ways to reduce the amount of energy we use.

needed. Energy efficiency refers to the amount of energy that is used to power a machine or
appliance, versus the amount of energy that is lost as heat.

Energy Debate Game
Game premise                                                                                                                                 Debate
Our “hypothetical” community receives its energy from an energy co-op. Every couple of
years the energy co-op evaluates its current energy portfolio and considers changes. This                                                                                                                                                         Energyyear, five groups are asking to make a presentation to the energy commission. There will be
a presentation on coal, natural gas, wind, solar, and nuclear energy.                                                                                                                               Local
The role of the energy commission                                                   P:
As a commissioner, you are asked to listen to the presentations and then ask questions (just
as would happen in a real community/city council meeting). After the commissioners arefinished with their questions, we will open the floor to citizens in the gallery. These citizens            Lesson
are actually students who will be making competing presentations so their questions may be
slanted towards their energy source, or they could be the type of comments you would hear
at a regular community meeting.

Process
At the end of the presentations and question/answer period, the commissioners will
adjourn to discuss and make their recommendations. While you are “discussing” the issues,
the classroom teacher will be conducting an assessment by asking the students probing
questions about the complex nature of our energy situation. The teacher will also ask them
to vote on how they think the commissioners will rule. This is a game, so some students
may vote for their energy source or they may feel strongly about another source. When you
return to the meeting, you will tell the students that you have decided to employ elements
of each of the energy sources presented:

  Coal – Because it is inexpensive and abundantly available
  Natural Gas – Because it is less expensive than coal and better for the environment
 Wind – Because it is renewable and usable for some smaller-scale applications
    in the community

  Solar – Because it is an abundant resource and renewable
  Nuclear – Because it is economical, safe, and cleaner for the environment than
    fossil fuels
